note_tweet.text:
A quick reminder on what SpaceX actually has in orbit, prompted by Elon's clarification today:

🛰️ Starshield = owned and controlled by the US government. Speed and usage limits are set by the US military and ultimately POTUS.
🌐 Starlink = a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX, limited to civilian or defensive use.

Two separate systems with two separate chains of control. Here's the whole SpaceX satellite lineup:

1️⃣ Starlink broadband (V2 Mini)
The largest satellite constellation ever built: about 11,100 working satellites in low Earth orbit and about 13,000 launched in total. Starlink serves more than 13 million customers in more than 150 countries and markets.

2️⃣ Starlink V3, launched by Starship
On Sept 28, Starship Flight 14 reached orbit for the first time and deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites. SpaceX made contact with every one of them. V3 is too big for Falcon 9, and each satellite adds about 1 Tbps of capacity, roughly 10x the satellites launched on Falcon 9. A future Starship can carry up to 60 at a time.

3️⃣ Starlink Mobile (Direct to Cell)
More than 650 satellites in orbit work like cell towers in space, connecting ordinary phones in dead zones. SpaceX says Direct to Cell has connected more than 12 million people. Last week the FCC approved up to 15,000 next-gen V2 Direct to Cell satellites, which SpaceX says will deliver more than 100x the bandwidth of the current system. They're backed by about 65 MHz of spectrum that SpaceX is buying from EchoStar.

4️⃣ Starshield
The government-owned version, built on Starlink technology. Dozens of satellites have been launched for the NRO's proliferated constellation, all on Falcon 9 from Vandenberg.

5️⃣ Laser mesh
Inter-satellite laser links route traffic across the constellation without a ground station under every satellite. This is what keeps ships, planes and remote communities connected.

6️⃣ Air, sea and communities
More than 150,000 vessels are connected. More than 1,400 commercial aircraft had Starlink installed in 2025. Community Gateways bring fiber-grade backhaul to isolated towns like Nome, Alaska.

7️⃣ Next: Orbital Data Centers
SpaceX has applied to the FCC for a system of up to 1 million solar-powered satellites built for AI compute in orbit and linked by optical lasers. The application is pending.

One company builds the rockets, the satellites, the lasers and the network. Nothing else comes close. 🚀

note_tweet.text:
You keep confusing a referendum with an automatic legal right to independence.

A referendum raises fundamental questions: Who is eligible to vote? Who determines the territory? What constitutional or negotiated framework governs the process? And who recognizes the outcome?

Kurdistan's 2017 referendum is precisely an example of why a vote alone does not guarantee statehood.

And before declaring "bye bye Yemen," perhaps explain who gets to speak for all southern Yemenis, including those who disagree with the separatist movement.

Self-determination is a serious principle of international law, not a shortcut that makes constitutional, political and international realities disappear.

You are entitled to advocate independence. You are not entitled to present your preferred outcome as an already established legal fact.
